lesson.title: Reading the Recipe: Mole-to-Mole Ratio Calculations
lesson.summary: Mole-to-mole calculations use the coefficients of a balanced equation directly as a conversion factor, turning the moles of one substance into the moles of any other substance in the same reaction.
lesson.body:
Stoichiometry introduced the mole ratio as the heart of every stoichiometry calculation, and Coefficients is where that ratio actually comes from: the whole number multipliers you place in front of each formula when balancing an equation. This chapter isolates that one step, converting moles of a given substance into moles of a desired substance, without yet worrying about converting to or from grams, which comes next.

The setup is always the same. Write the balanced equation. Identify how many moles of the given substance you have, and identify the substance you want to find. Build a conversion factor from the two coefficients, the desired substance's coefficient on top, the given substance's coefficient on the bottom, so that the units of the given substance cancel and you are left with units of the desired substance.

Return to the combustion of propane from the Combustion Reactions chapter: C3H8(g) + 5 O2(g) -> 3 CO2(g) + 4 H2O(g), already confirmed balanced with 3 carbons, 8 hydrogens, and 10 oxygens on each side. Suppose 2.50 mol of C3H8 burns completely. How many moles of CO2 form, and how many moles of O2 are consumed in the process? For carbon dioxide, use the ratio of 3 mol CO2 to 1 mol C3H8 from the coefficients: 2.50 mol C3H8 times, 3 mol CO2 divided by 1 mol C3H8, equals 7.50 mol CO2. For oxygen, use the ratio of 5 mol O2 to 1 mol C3H8: 2.50 mol C3H8 times, 5 mol O2 divided by 1 mol C3H8, equals 12.5 mol O2.

A common error is flipping the ratio upside down, which throws the answer off completely. This is easy to catch if you check that your units actually cancel before you multiply. Writing out the unit cancellation explicitly, mol C3H8 in the denominator canceling with mol C3H8 in your starting quantity, is a small habit that prevents most mole ratio mistakes.
